name: Maltego
purpose: Commercial link-analysis platform with a graph interface and a transform ecosystem that queries data sources — infrastructure, corporate, social, breach and commercial intelligence — and expands entities into a visual graph.
journalism_use_case: The commercial benchmark for graph-based investigation: start from a name, domain or company and expand through transforms to related entities, building a visual network. Many OSINT training curricula teach it, so a newsroom hiring an experienced investigator may inherit it as an expectation.
pros: Transform ecosystem is the product: hundreds of integrated data sources queried through one interface, which no open tool matches for breadth of commercial data
Graph-first interface suits investigative reasoning and is genuinely effective for exploring entity relationships interactively
Established in the field with extensive training material, so an experienced investigator is likely to be productive immediately
Credit-based model means light use can be genuinely cheap, including a free Community Edition tier
cons: NOT open source: proprietary software with a credit-metered pricing model, and the costs are substantial at professional tiers — Entry EUR3,000/year (10,000 credits/month, includes Hunchly) and Professional EUR7,500/year (20,000-40,000 credits/month, up to 5 users, billed per seat), with Enterprise quote-only (all verified on the vendor pricing page 2026-11-16)

Every transform query discloses your target to Maltego and to the underlying data provider — for a surveillance-industry investigation that is a material exposure, and the convenience of the interface makes it easy to forget
Community Edition is restricted to graph-only use with 200 or 1,000 credits per month, which is enough to learn the tool and not to run an investigation
Credit consumption is hard to predict, so budgeting is awkward and an exploratory session can consume a month's allowance
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Pricing verified on the vendor page 2026-11-16 and recorded in sources/recovered/cat/pricing.tsv: Basic free forever (200 credits/month) or Basic+ (1,000 credits/month), Community Edition graph only; Entry EUR3,000/year including Hunchly; Professional EUR7,500/year, up to 5 users, billed per seat; Enterprise custom quote for 5+ users. Maltego's prominence in OSINT training is well documented.
assessment: Reference only for your profile, and deliberately so: the open chain in this catalogue (subfinder, httpx, asn, certstream, NetworkX, Gephi) covers most of what Maltego's infrastructure transforms do, at no licence cost and without disclosing your targets to a commercial platform. The case for buying it is an experienced investigator who is already fast in it, or a specific commercial data source you cannot otherwise reach. If you do, budget per-seat annually and treat every transform as a disclosure.
maintenance_evidence: Commercial product under continuous vendor development; pricing page verified live 2026-11-16 with current tier structure. No repository to assess — maintenance is inferred from the operating commercial service and active vendor documentation, which is the only evidence available for proprietary software.
licence: Proprietary commercial licence; Community Edition is a restricted free tier
model_or_data_licence: Transform data comes from many providers under their own terms, several of which restrict redistribution of results.
licence_restrictions: Proprietary throughout. Data-provider terms restrict republication of transform results, which matters if a graph is the basis of a published graphic.
costs: Verified 2026-11-16 from the vendor pricing page: Basic free forever (200 credits/month) or Basic+ (1,000 credits/month), Community Edition graph only; Entry EUR3,000/year (10,000 credits/month, includes Hunchly); Professional EUR7,500/year (20,000-40,000 credits/month, up to 5 users, billed per seat); Enterprise custom quote (5+ users). Credits are consumed per transform, so operating cost scales with investigation intensity and is hard to forecast.
privacy: The weakest point for investigative use: every transform discloses your target entity to Maltego and to the underlying data provider, continuously through an investigation. For work on a surveillance vendor or a state actor, that is an exposure the open alternatives avoid.
alternatives: The open chain: subfinder plus httpx plus asn plus certstream for discovery, NetworkX for analysis, Gephi for visualisation — no licence cost and no target disclosure
SpiderFoot for automated open-source breadth, accepting its own disclosure footprint
Hunchly (bundled with Maltego Entry) separately, for browsing-session capture
blockers: Proprietary with substantial per-seat annual cost; every transform discloses investigation targets to the vendor and data providers
summary: Commercial link-analysis platform with a graph interface and a transform ecosystem that queries data sources — infrastructure…
oss_detail: Hosted service or proprietary software — governed by service terms, not a software licence
software_price_note: Community Edition free forever (200 credits/month, graph only); Entry EUR 3,000/year (incl. Hunchly); Professional EUR 7,500/year per seat, up to 5 users; Enterprise quote (verified 2026-11-16)

name: Timesketch
purpose: Collaborative forensic timeline-analysis platform where investigators import timestamped events from many sources, search and filter them, tag and comment on entries, and build a shared narrative timeline.
journalism_use_case: Building a shared, evidenced chronology on a complex investigation: import timestamped events from documents, logs, flight records, filings and messages, then let several reporters tag, annotate and query them together — which is how a multi-strand investigation's timeline stops living in one person's notebook.
pros: Collaborative timeline analysis is a genuine gap in newsroom tooling: every complex investigation needs a chronology, and almost all of them are maintained as a document that goes stale
Tagging and commenting on individual events with attribution means the timeline carries its own evidence and reasoning, which is what makes it defensible later
Apache-2.0 and self-hostable, actively maintained by Google's security team with real production use in incident response
Search and filtering over large event sets means the timeline scales past what a document can hold
cons: Designed for digital forensics and incident response, so the import formats and vocabulary assume log data rather than documents, filings and human events — adapting it to journalistic sources means writing importers
Operational commitment: OpenSearch plus PostgreSQL plus the application, comparable to running a search platform
Corporate-maintained open source with no commercial obligation to the project, so continuity depends on one team's priorities within a large company
The learning curve and forensic framing will deter the reporters who would most benefit from a shared timeline
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived under Google maintenance. Timesketch's use in digital forensics and incident response is well documented; journalism use is uncommon and unverified here.
assessment: Worth piloting on one complex investigation, specifically because the shared-chronology problem is real and under-served — but expect to write importers to get journalistic sources in. For your profile the pragmatic alternative is a disciplined Datasette-over-SQLite timeline with a fixed schema, which lacks the collaborative tagging but costs a day rather than a deployment. Choose Timesketch if the investigation is long and several people need to work the chronology together.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived under Google's maintenance with continuing development. Corporate-maintained open source with production use in incident response; continuity depends on internal priorities rather than a foundation.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure: OpenSearch plus PostgreSQL plus the application — one well-provisioned VM minimum, more as event volume grows. Importer development is the other real cost. Estimate.
privacy: Self-hosted; timeline data and annotations stay internal. The timeline will contain your investigative reasoning as well as evidence, so it is a sensitive artefact deserving the same protection as source material.
alternatives: A structured SQLite timeline published with Datasette, which is far cheaper and lacks collaboration features
A shared spreadsheet with a fixed schema and discipline, which is what most investigations actually use
Aeon Timeline or similar commercial tools, accepting proprietary software and local-only storage
summary: Collaborative forensic timeline-analysis platform where investigators import timestamped events from many sources…

name: DVC (Data Version Control)
purpose: Version-control system for data and machine-learning pipelines that tracks large files and datasets alongside git, with reproducible pipeline definitions, remote storage backends and experiment tracking.
journalism_use_case: Provenance for investigative datasets: a leak extraction, a cleaned registry and a derived analysis each versioned and reproducible, so six months later you can show exactly which version of which dataset produced a published figure — and re-run the pipeline to confirm it.
pros: Solves the reproducibility problem that quietly undermines data journalism: datasets change, cleaning scripts evolve, and without versioning a published figure cannot be reproduced even by its author
Pipeline definitions make the transformation chain from raw to published explicit, which doubles as a methodology description you can share with an editor or a reader
Works alongside git rather than replacing it, so the workflow is familiar and the data stays out of the repository
Apache-2.0 with remote-storage support including S3-compatible and local backends, so sensitive data need not touch a commercial cloud
cons: Repository transferred from Iterative to Treeverse (verified by redirect 2026-11-17), following corporate change — governance continuity is a monitoring item for infrastructure you would depend on for years, and pinned URLs should be updated
Conceptual overhead: DVC's pipeline and cache model takes real learning, and for a single analysis a documented script plus a dated data copy achieves much of the benefit
Designed for machine-learning workflows, so some concepts (experiments, metrics) map awkwardly onto investigative data work
Remote storage configuration is where sensitive data could leak to a commercial backend by default — the configuration needs deliberate attention
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. The documented finding from this session: iterative/dvc redirects to treeverse/dvc (verified 2026-11-17, recorded in leads.md L4), following Iterative's acquisition — a governance change rather than a licence change, with the project remaining Apache-2.0 per the API.
assessment: Worth adopting if you run recurring data pipelines and want published figures to be reproducible — which is a standard you should want. For your profile the lighter alternative deserves consideration first: a dated immutable copy of each input dataset plus a scripted, version-controlled transformation achieves most of the provenance benefit with no new tooling. Adopt DVC when pipelines become complex enough that the manual discipline fails. Point storage at infrastructure you control and update references to the treeverse path.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: live and non-archived at treeverse/dvc with the iterative/dvc path redirecting, Apache-2.0 per the API. Active development continues under the new organisation; the governance transfer is the item to monitor rather than a maintenance concern today.
costs: No fee. Remote storage costs depend on the backend — object storage you control, or a commercial provider at their rates (not priced here). Compute is negligible. Estimate.
privacy: Data stays wherever you point the remote. The risk is a default or convenient configuration sending sensitive datasets to a commercial cloud backend — configure local or self-hosted S3-compatible storage deliberately.
alternatives: Dated immutable data copies plus version-controlled transformation scripts — the low-tech approach that often suffices
git-annex or git-lfs for large-file versioning without the pipeline model
Snakemake or a Makefile for reproducible pipelines without data versioning
summary: Version-control system for data and machine-learning pipelines that tracks large files and datasets alongside git…

name: Quarto
purpose: Publishing system that renders documents combining prose with executable Python, R and Julia code into HTML, PDF, Word and websites, with cross-references, citations and parameterised reports.
journalism_use_case: Publishing a methodology alongside a story: a Quarto document contains the prose explanation, the actual analysis code and the figures it produces, rendered as a web page readers can inspect — which turns 'we analysed the data' into a verifiable account of how.
pros: Executable documents mean the published methodology cannot drift from the analysis that produced the figures, which is the failure mode of hand-written methodology notes
Multi-language support (Python, R) means a mixed newsroom can use one publishing system, and R matters here because much media-analysis methodology is written in it
MIT licensed with very active development and strong commercial backing from Posit, plus excellent documentation
Renders to HTML, PDF and websites from one source, so the same analysis serves a public methodology page and an internal memo
cons: Commercial backing by Posit means direction follows their strategy, though the MIT licence and large community limit lock-in risk
Rendering toolchain (Pandoc, LaTeX for PDF, language runtimes) is heavy, and reproducible rendering across machines needs containerisation
Publishing a methodology document exposes your analysis to scrutiny, which is the point and also a discipline — sloppy code published is worse than no code published
Learning curve for the cross-reference and citation features, though basic use is immediate
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived with very active development under Posit's maintenance. Quarto's adoption in data science and academic publishing is well established; its use for journalism methodology notes is a natural extension.
assessment: Adopt it for methodology publication — this is the tool that makes 'show your work' practical, and for an outlet whose findings will be attacked, a published reproducible methodology is a strong defensive asset. For your profile I would make it standard practice for any data-driven story: the Quarto document is written as the analysis proceeds, published alongside the piece, and containerised so a reader with the data can reproduce the figures.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived with very active development under Posit PBC's commercial maintenance and a large user community across data science and academia.
costs: No fee. Rendering toolchain is a local install; LaTeX for PDF output is a large dependency. Negligible infrastructure beyond web hosting for published output. Estimate.
privacy: Local rendering. The consideration is editorial rather than technical: a published methodology document reveals your data sources and analytical choices, which is usually desirable and occasionally discloses more about a source than intended — review before publishing.
alternatives: Jupyter notebooks published as HTML, which is simpler and less polished
Observable or a hand-written methodology page, which drifts from the code
R Markdown for R-only workflows, which Quarto supersedes
summary: Publishing system that renders documents combining prose with executable Python, R and Julia code into HTML, PDF…

name: Frictionless Data (frictionless-py)
purpose: Python framework implementing the Frictionless Data specifications for describing, validating, extracting and transforming tabular datasets, with schema inference and detailed validation reports.
journalism_use_case: Publishing a dataset with a schema and a validation report: when you release the data behind an investigation, a Data Package declares the fields, types and constraints and proves the data conforms — which pre-empts the 'your data is wrong' response and makes the dataset reusable by others.
pros: Validation reports are a concrete quality artefact: publishing one alongside a dataset demonstrates that you checked types, missing values and constraints rather than asserting the data is clean
Schema declaration makes a published dataset genuinely reusable, which is how an investigation's data becomes a resource other journalists build on
Open specification with multiple language implementations, so a Data Package you publish is consumable without your toolchain
Open Knowledge Foundation stewardship aligns with open-data publication rather than a commercial product
cons: Tabular data only, so documents, graphs and media collections are out of scope — it addresses one slice of investigative data publication
Adoption outside the open-data community is modest, so a Data Package is less immediately recognisable to a general audience than a plain CSV plus a readme
Schema inference is a starting point that needs human correction, and an auto-inferred schema published uncorrected can misdescribe the data
Maintenance cadence is steady rather than brisk, consistent with specification-implementation work
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived under Open Knowledge Foundation stewardship. Frictionless adoption in the open-data community is documented by the project; journalism adoption is modest and unverified here.
assessment: Integrate it when you publish datasets, which for an accountability outlet should be routine — the validation report plus declared schema is cheap to produce and materially raises the credibility and reusability of a released dataset. For your profile the minimum viable version is worth doing even without the framework: publish a schema description, a validation summary and a stated provenance for every dataset you release, and frictionless-py simply makes that systematic.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived under Open Knowledge Foundation stewardship with steady rather than frequent development, consistent with implementing a stable specification. Classified stable-low.
licence: MIT (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
model_or_data_licence: n/a. The specifications themselves are openly licensed.
privacy: Local processing. The consideration is what you publish: a validation report describes your data's structure, which is usually harmless and occasionally reveals more about collection methods than intended.
alternatives: Great Expectations for heavier data-validation pipelines
A hand-written schema and readme alongside a CSV, which is the practical minimum
CSV on the Web standards for a W3C-aligned alternative
summary: Python framework implementing the Frictionless Data specifications for describing, validating…

name: OpenTimestamps
purpose: Client for creating and verifying trustless timestamp proofs anchored in the Bitcoin blockchain, attesting that a file existed at a given time without relying on a trusted timestamping authority.
journalism_use_case: Proving when you received material without revealing it: timestamp the hash of a leaked document on receipt, and you can later demonstrate that you held that exact file from that date — which matters if the authenticity or the timing of your acquisition is challenged, and which discloses nothing because only the hash is published.
pros: Hash-only anchoring means you prove possession at a time without disclosing content — exactly the property source protection requires, and a notarisation service cannot offer

Trustless verification: the proof depends on the Bitcoin blockchain rather than on a company that must still exist and be trusted when you need it, which for a decade-long legal horizon is a real advantage
Free to use with no account, so timestamping every received document at ingest costs nothing and requires no relationship
Simple and auditable: the proof format is specified and verifiable independently of the original client
cons: Proves existence at a time, nothing more: it says nothing about where a document came from, whether it is authentic, or who made it — and a published claim must be precise about that narrow meaning
Confirmation waits on Bitcoin block inclusion, so a proof takes hours to become complete — fine for ingest, not for a same-hour claim
Depends on public calendar servers for aggregation, so your hash submissions are visible to those operators (the hash only, not the content)
Niche and single-maintainer-adjacent, with modest activity; the specification's durability matters more than the client's
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived. OpenTimestamps is an established approach to trustless timestamping with a published specification; journalism use is uncommon and unverified here.
assessment: Integrate it into document ingest — timestamping the hash of every received file is a few lines in a pipeline and gives you an evidentiary property you cannot retrofit. For your profile the specific scenario it addresses is a government later claiming a document was fabricated after an event: a timestamp proof from the date of receipt rebuts that directly. Be precise in any published claim about what it proves, which is possession of that exact file at that time and nothing else.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived with modest activity. Classified stable-low: the specification and proof format are the durable artefacts, and the client is small and feature-complete, so low velocity carries less risk than usual.
licence: LGPL-3.0 (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
licence_restrictions: LGPL permits linking from your own tooling provided the library remains replaceable.
costs: Free. No Bitcoin transaction fee for the user — the calendar servers aggregate submissions. Negligible compute.
privacy: Only the hash is submitted, so content is never disclosed — the property that makes it usable on source material. The calendar operators see your hash submissions and their timing, which reveals that you timestamped something on a date, not what.
alternatives: A commercial trusted timestamping authority (RFC 3161), which is faster and requires trusting a company
Publishing a hash in a dated public venue, which is cruder and still effective
Sigstore for signing rather than timestamping
summary: Client for creating and verifying trustless timestamp proofs anchored in the Bitcoin blockchain, attesting…

name: unitedstates/congress
purpose: Collection of scrapers and parsers for US Congressional data — bills, votes, amendments, committee activity and member information — producing structured JSON from official sources.
journalism_use_case: Tracking US federal legislation systematically: who sponsored a surveillance bill, how committee membership shaped it, which amendments were quietly added — the structured record that makes legislative accountability reporting possible without reading the Congressional Record by hand.
pros: Structured output from official sources means the data is authoritative and the parsing is auditable — important when a story turns on who voted how
Covers amendments and committee activity, not just final votes, which is where legislative influence actually operates and where most coverage stops
Public-domain or permissively licensed civic-tech project with a long history, feeding several downstream services
Free against free official sources, so the whole capability costs only compute
cons: Civic-tech community maintenance means activity is episodic and depends on volunteer attention — a real continuity question for a scraping project against changing official sites
US federal only
Congressional data structures are genuinely complex (bill versions, amendment trees, procedural votes), so the structured output still requires domain knowledge to interpret correctly
Several downstream services (GovTrack, ProPublica's congress API historically) wrap this data more conveniently, so direct use is often unnecessary
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived under the unitedstates civic-tech project. Its role as an upstream source for several congressional-data services is documented by those projects.
assessment: Integrate it if you cover US federal legislation and need the structured record, but check first whether a downstream API gives you the same data with less work. For your profile the broader transferable point is the same as for openstates and querido-diario: legislative accountability depends on structured records, and where your jurisdiction does not publish them, building the collection is a durable public good as well as a reporting asset.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived under civic-tech community maintenance with episodic activity. Classified stable-low: a long-lived project whose maintenance depends on volunteer attention, which is a continuity consideration for scraper-based collection.
licence: Public domain / CC0 (unitedstates project convention — confirm from the repository licence file)
model_or_data_licence: Congressional records are US government public records.
licence_restrictions: None material — the unitedstates project convention is public-domain dedication, which is unusually permissive.
costs: No fee. Negligible compute; the real cost is scraper maintenance if you extend it. Estimate.
privacy: Public records; scraping official sites is unremarkable.
alternatives: GovTrack or a congressional-data API for the same data with less maintenance
openstates-scrapers for state rather than federal legislatures
Congress.gov directly for one-off lookups
blockers: US federal only; volunteer maintenance against changing official sites
summary: Collection of scrapers and parsers for US Congressional data — bills, votes, amendments…
